title: europes renewables boom is becoming gas demand bust 2026 08 13
author: Gavin Maguire
text:
LITTLETON, Colorado, Aug 13 (Reuters) - The defining question of Europe's energy story over the past few years has been whether the region has enough gas. That query is starting to look outdated.
Following Russia's invasion of Ukraine, policymakers, utilities and traders became fixated on storage levels, LNG cargo arrivals and winter weather forecasts. Gas inventories became the key ​measure of Europe's energy security.
But a new trend emerging across the continent's power system suggests Europe may increasingly be asking the wrong question.
The issue is no longer ‌whether Europe can secure enough gas supplies. It is whether Europe still needs as much gas as it once did.
Combined electricity generation from Europe's wind and solar farms is on track to exceed output from gas-fired power plants for the longest stretch on record in 2026.
That may sound like just another clean-energy milestone. In reality, it could mark a structural shift in Europe's gas market.
A decade ago, gas routinely generated more than twice as ​much electricity as the combined output from Europe's wind and solar fleet.
In 2016, combined monthly output from solar and wind generally hovered between 30 and 45 terawatt hours (TWh), while gas-fired ​generation often exceeded 100 TWh, data from energy think tank Ember shows.
Today the gap has vanished.
Combined solar and wind output has climbed to around 80-110 ⁠terawatt hours a month while gas-fired generation has steadily lost ground.
Throughout much of 2025 and 2026, renewable generation has matched or exceeded gas output for extended periods.
Crucially, this is not simply the ​result of favourable weather.
Europe's gas-fired generation capacity has grown only modestly over the past quarter century, from 250 gigawatts to around 400 GW. Wind and solar capacity, meanwhile, has surged from under 20 GW ​to nearly 750 GW over the same period.
Europe now has nearly twice as much installed wind and solar capacity as gas-fired capacity.
That distinction matters.
Temporary shifts in generation can be explained by weather. Structural shifts are driven by changes in the footprint of the generation fleet itself.
Europe has spent two decades steadily constructing a power system built around renewable resources rather than fossil fuels.
Once sufficient renewable capacity is installed, declining fossil generation becomes less a policy aspiration than ​a mathematical consequence.
What the data suggest is that Europe may have crossed that threshold.
Seasonal generation data may be even more revealing.
Historically, gas served as the workhorse of Europe's ​power system, with demand easing in spring and summer before rising sharply in winter.
Now wind and solar are increasingly dominating the April-through-October period.
In 2026, renewable generation has reached record highs while coal and gas generation have fallen ‌to multi-year ⁠lows. The traditional gas-burn season is becoming progressively shorter as renewables supply a growing share of electricity demand.
For gas markets, that is potentially transformative.
Every month that renewables dominate power supply reduces gas consumption, lowers gas import requirements and chips away at one of the largest sources of European gas demand.
The most important implication may be for gas inventories.
Since 2022, Europe has treated storage as a critical insurance policy against supply disruptions and winter demand surges.
But if power-sector gas demand keeps shrinking, Europe may not need to inject as much gas into storage each summer or withdraw as much during ​winter.
Storage will remain essential during cold spells and ​periods of weak renewable output. But as ⁠wind and solar continue to displace gas generation, the continent's underlying need for gas inventories may gradually decline as well.
This changes the debate from "Does Europe have enough gas?" to "How much gas does Europe actually need?"
The broader historical picture reinforces the trend.
Coal dominated Europe's energy system from the ​1960s before giving way to natural gas, which became the principal replacement fuel for power generation and industry in the 1990s.
Now renewables are mounting ​a similar challenge to gas.
For ⁠years, policymakers described gas as a bridge fuel between coal and renewables.
Europe's power system increasingly looks as though it is approaching the far side of that bridge.
With every new wind farm and solar park, Europe is not merely producing cleaner electricity. It is steadily reducing the amount of gas it needs to import, store and burn.
And for a continent that spent years worrying about whether it could secure enough of the ⁠fuel to ​get through winter, needing less gas in the first place may prove the most consequential energy development of all.
